extracted.intended_audience: DARPA proposers and prospective I2O program managers (industry, academia, and government practitioners)
extracted.subtask_short: I2O proposers and PM hiring guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Office-level Q&A providing guidance for proposers and prospective program managers about transition processes, hiring/evaluation practices, priority technical areas, and program-security/practical recruitment steps within DARPA I2O. Covers how DARPA evaluates transition readiness and how I2O recruits and assesses PM candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition Council funding-approval criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition Council approves funding for existing programs that have satisfied the DARPA 'technical miracle' and are now in the 'how do we scale the impact' conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transition is a spectrum from program of record to purely commercial activities; Transition Council is a decision-making process distinct from the Tech Council (which approves funding for new programs). Transition Council focuses on scaling impact and may provide additional resources when programs have demonstrated technical success but need help scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACO-T transition support function
rubrics_metrics.description: ACO-T is a transition support function within the Adaptive Capabilities Office created to help program managers navigate more complex transition pathways beyond the traditional program-of-record route.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transition paths can be to a program of record, a specific military transition, commercial activities, or anything in between; ACO-T exists because some transitions require different management forms than core tech offices can provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency-level integrated approach to transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition cannot be treated purely as a single PM activity; achieving large-scale transitions often requires a DARPA-wide, integrated, top-down effort engaging leadership (Director, Deputy Secretary of Defense) to navigate institutional processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because program managers alone have limited bandwidth, DARPA pursues agency-scale activities and decision processes (e.g., Transition Council) to push transitions through institutional channels and scale impact across the Department of Defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial pitch: answer first three Heilmeier Catechism questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates asked to submit a sample pitch that answers the first three Heilmeier Catechism questions in 1–2 short paragraphs: (1) What are you trying to do? (2) How is it done today? (3) What is new about your approach and why do you think it might succeed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch should demonstrate a broad understanding of the state of the art and a 'glimmer' that the problem might be solvable (unrealistic-sounding ideas with no solvability are insufficient, e.g., Star Trek transporter without grounding). DARPA iterates on the draft to develop well-grounded answers to those questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment: willingness to take feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: One assessment criterion is whether the candidate is willing to take feedback; nobody arrives at DARPA with all necessary PM skills, and the ability to accept and incorporate feedback is critical to success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruiters/PMs will iterate with candidates on their written pitches; responsiveness and constructive iteration on feedback are evaluated during this process and in interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment: communication and persuasion skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Program managers must be able to communicate and motivate others to do technical work; poor communication undermines success as a PM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation includes written pitch clarity and oral interview performance. Communication ability is judged by whether candidates can motivate teams, explain ideas, and present multiple ideas coherently to peers and leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment: idea-generation breadth (not a one-trick pony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates are asked about other ideas they have to assess their ability to create ideas beyond a single concept—i.e., to ensure they aren't a 'one trick pony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewers probe for additional relevant ideas after reviewing the candidate's pitch to evaluate creativity, breadth, and sustained ideation capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring/interview sequence and evaluative checkpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical process: express interest -> submit Heilmeier-based pitch -> iterate on draft -> meet with office PMs and deputy -> meet with DARPA director; there is a set of criteria used at each stage reflecting pitch quality, responsiveness, communication, idea breadth, and alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is used to evaluate both written materials and interview performance; successful candidates advance through staged interactions with PMs, office leadership, and agency leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority hiring need: AI PMs with national-security understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: I2O is shortest on AI PMs and is most focused on recruiting high-quality people who understand AI and national security ramifications (not merely 'apply AI to a problem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desired candidates should understand broader AI risks (e.g., AGI, agents run amok) and defenses; expertise in applying AI is useful, but priority is on thinking through national-security implications and defense strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal methods-based Authority to Operate (ATO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a formal methods-based ATO process tied to actual artifacts (code, architecture descriptions) instead of the traditional labor-intensive, paper-oriented ATO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal-methods ATO can produce required paperwork in days instead of months and can regenerate paperwork when artifacts change. Practices include tying ATO to architecture descriptions, using generated crypto proven correct, replacing parsers with generated parsers, and focusing remediation on the most important components identified via formal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red teaming and realistic cyber demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Take red teaming far more seriously by performing real, demonstrable effects rather than only white-carding or writing reports about what cyber could do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real demonstrations (the speaker provocatively suggests causing an observable failure to compel attention) are recommended to make stakeholders take cyber risks seriously; the emphasis is on evidence-backed demonstrations rather than hypothetical reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent acquisition and retention practices to mitigate classification/compensation barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Make efforts to reduce barriers to participation: perform as much work as possible at the unclassified level, use DARPA Connect to reach more people, and work to streamline security and IT requirements so collaboration is less onerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize intrinsic motivations beyond pay (mission-driven recruits). Acknowledge constraints outside DARPA control (e.g., certifying SCIF space). Request proposers provide specific pain points to help improve processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of emerging technical challenge: PAI/CAI surveillance ecosystem
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAI/CAI surveillance ecosystem (commercially available aggregated data that allows adversaries to track people) is cited as a hard-to-solve problem and a priority area to explore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solutions could be regulatory (restrict aggregation) or technical mitigations to prevent perfect tracking; DARPA is soliciting input/ideas in this domain and invites proposers to suggest approaches.
